haiku-low.q1: No. Cursor updates go through the Redis pres:{doc} channel and the cursor script. They never touch the document service or Postgres.
haiku-low.q2: The client sends at most one cursor every 60 ms, with the last position trailing, plus one repeat 250 ms after the caret stops. The server accepts one per 50 ms per connection and silently drops faster updates, giving them no seq.
haiku-low.q3: It keeps the cursor as pending for that connId and leaves the shown caret where it is. It draws the caret once appliedRev catches up to that revision.
haiku-low.q4: If its seq is not higher than the last seq seen for that connection, it is dropped. Otherwise it is drawn at appliedRev via transformPosition, and if that throws HistoryGone the position is dropped and the current caret stays.
haiku-low.q5: Each connection has its own caret keyed by connId, all in the user's colour, so two tabs show two carets. The user disappears only when their last connection is removed; closing one tab sends only cursor_gone.
haiku-low.q6: After a clean tab close, within milliseconds, well under 2 s. After a node crash, under 45 s: 30 to 40 s until a sweep, plus delivery.
haiku-low.q7: In Redis, per doc: a ZSET of userId/connId presence members, a HASH of last cursor per connId, and a pub/sub channel. Heartbeats every 10 s refresh scores and key TTLs of 60 s.
haiku-low.q8: A surviving node's heartbeat sweep removes members whose score is over 30 s old, publishing cursor_gone and presence absent. That node then sends those events to its own clients, and other nodes get them via Redis.
haiku-low.q9: Both go through the Redis pres:{doc} channel: the other node receives it and forwards it to its local sockets. The sending connection is skipped, so the sender's own node gets no echo.
haiku-low.q10: The node subscribes to pres:{doc} before reading the snapshot and queues events for the new connection until the snapshot is sent. It then sends the queued events in order.
haiku-low.q11: The snapshot includes stored last cursors, so the joiner sees them. An idle sender re-sends its caret every 10 s whenever its appliedRev has moved, which keeps stored cursors current.
haiku-low.q12: Any cursor with seq not above the last seq for its connId is dropped, so older or duplicate updates never move it back. Newer updates with a higher rev are held as pending until applied.

sonnet.q1: No. Cursor updates never touch the document service or Postgres. They go from the gateway node to Redis (the cursor script), which stores them and publishes them on pres:{doc}.
sonnet.q2: The client throttles to one cursor every 60 ms, always sending the last position, and re-sends the final position after 250 ms once the caret stops. The server checks 50 ms per connection on arrival. It drops faster updates silently and gives them no seq.
sonnet.q3: It holds the cursor as pending[connId] and leaves the shown caret where it is. Once appliedRev reaches that rev (after an ack or remote_op), it draws it. Only the newest pending update is held.
sonnet.q4: If its seq is not higher than lastSeq it is dropped. If its rev is older than appliedRev, the position is moved with transformPosition(pos, rev, appliedRev) and drawn. If that throws (HistoryGone), the position is dropped and the caret already shown stays.
sonnet.q5: Each tab is its own connection with its own caret, keyed by connId. Both carets have the same colour (by userId). The user stays listed as present while any connection remains. They disappear (presence absent) only when their last connection is removed. Closing one tab sends only cursor_gone.
sonnet.q6: After a clean tab close it is milliseconds, well under 2 s. After a node crash it is 30 to 40 s, under 45 s.
sonnet.q7: In the Redis the team already runs. Presence is per connection (userId/connId) in the ZSET pres:conns:{doc}, with scores from Redis TIME. Cursors are per connection in the HASH pres:cur:{doc}. Events go on the pres:{doc} channel. Each node's heartbeat script refreshes entries every 10 s by updating the score and the 60 s key TTL. Cursors are refreshed by new cursor updates and by idle clients re-sending when appliedRev has moved.
sonnet.q8: Nothing cleans up at crash time. The heartbeat script run by any surviving node on that doc sweeps members whose score is older than 30 s. It removes them, deletes their cursor, and publishes cursor_gone and presence absent (if no other connection of that user). The surviving gateway nodes forward these to their clients. If no node survives, the key TTL of 60 s expires the keys.
sonnet.q9: The cursor script publishes on Redis channel pres:{doc}. Every node subscribed to it gets the event and forwards it to its local sockets on that doc. The sender's own node also receives it but skips the sending connection, so there is no echo. Other local viewers on that node get it.
sonnet.q10: The node subscribes to pres:{doc} before reading the snapshot. The join script atomically registers the connection and returns the members and cursors. The node queues events for the new connection, sends the snapshot, then the queued events in order, then forwards live. Events are absolute state and ordered. Queued cursors are dropped by seq or followed by their cursor_gone.
sonnet.q11: The snapshot returned by the join script includes the stored last cursor of every connection. Idle clients re-send their caret every 10 s when appliedRev has moved, and also send once after load. So stored cursors stay near head and the joiner draws them via transformPosition.
sonnet.q12: The receiver keeps lastSeq per connId and ignores any cursor whose seq is not greater (older or duplicate). The gateway node is the single writer of seq, and a higher seq never carries a lower rev. Redis only stores a cursor if its seq is higher.
